nodes.label: Coral reef research

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_000
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was the purpose of the biopsy collected from each tagged coral colony?
nodes.answer: The purpose of the biopsy was to collect samples for symbiont community identification in the absence of recent heat stress.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_001
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the study described in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main focus is to assess the heat tolerance of coral populations and its relation to predicting bleaching outcomes during active coral restoration efforts.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What coral species was studied in the research?
nodes.answer: The coral species studied is Montipora capitata.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_003
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main hypothesis supported by the research regarding heat tolerance in corals?
nodes.answer: The research supports the notion that heat tolerance is a complex trait with detectable partitioning of its underlying sources.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What species of coral was studied in K ne ohe Bay?
nodes.answer: The species studied was Montipora capitata.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_005
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What was the purpose of assessing survivorship several months post-heat stress?
nodes.answer: The purpose was to evaluate the survivorship of the remaining coral fragments after exposure to heat stress.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_006
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Why are juvenile COTS difficult to study?
nodes.answer: Juvenile COTS are difficult to study because they are cryptic in the reef infrastructure, making them hard to observe and analyze.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_007
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was the main objective of the study outlined in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main objective was to understand rates and patterns of symbiont turnover under ambient (non-stressful) conditions in corals.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_008
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How many coral species were investigated in this study?
nodes.answer: Six Caribbean reef-building coral species were investigated.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_009
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What method was used to measure the symbiont/host cell ratios in coral tissue?
nodes.answer: Quantitative PCR was used to measure the symbiont/host cell ratios in coral tissue.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_010
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the significance of the findings regarding coral-Symbiodiniaceae homeostasis?
nodes.answer: The findings provide insights into the mechanisms of coral-algal symbiosis and dysbiosis, which are important for understanding coral health and restoration approaches.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_011
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the research discussed in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main focus is on quantifying diel expulsion rates of symbionts under ambient conditions across various Caribbean reef-building coral species.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_012
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What method did the researchers develop to study symbiont expulsion?
nodes.answer: They developed a lab-based assay to quantify diel expulsion rates from replicate coral fragments.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_013
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What insight do the researchers hope to gain from their results?
nodes.answer: They hope to gain insights into the mechanisms driving symbiont turnover and community composition, which can inform future work on coral-algal symbiosis during bleaching and recovery.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_014
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What have laboratory studies documented regarding juvenile COTS?
nodes.answer: Laboratory studies have documented their development and transition to a coral diet.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_015
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Where were the adult COTS collected for the study?
nodes.answer: The adults were collected near Cairns, in the northern Great Barrier Reef (GBR).
